extracted.intended_audience: writers, editors, researchers, and students preparing Chicago Notes and Bibliography citations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for formatting names, titles, and full citations (especially books, chapters, editors, translators, pseudonyms, non-English works, and special cases) following the Chicago Manual of Style Notes & Bibliography rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudonyms (notation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a work is attributed to an invented or descriptive name, and the author’s real name is not known, pseud. (roman, in brackets) may follow the name, especially if it might not be immediately clear to readers that the name is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In text citations or shortened notes, pseud. is usually omitted. Examples: AK Muckraker [pseud.]. “Palin Is Back at Work.”; Centinel [pseud.]. Letters. If the pseudonym is widely used, it may be treated as the author’s real name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Widely used pseudonym treated as real name
rubrics_metrics.description: A widely used pseudonym is generally treated as if it were the author’s real name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List the work under the pseudonym as the author (e.g., Eliot, George.; Twain, Mark.). If the real name is of interest, it may follow in brackets (see separate rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Real name following pseudonym in brackets
rubrics_metrics.description: The real name, if of interest to readers, may follow the pseudonym in brackets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Jay-Z [Shawn Carter]. Decoded. If the real name is better known than the pseudonym, use the real name and put the pseudonym in brackets followed by pseud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer real name when better known
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author’s real name is better known than the pseudonym, the real name should be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If needed, include the pseudonym in brackets, followed by pseud. Example: Brontë, Charlotte [Currer Bell, pseud.]. Jane Eyre. In text or shortened citations, the pseud. is usually omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-references for pseudonyms and alternative listing
rubrics_metrics.description: If a bibliography includes works by the same author under different pseudonyms, list them under the real name with pseudonyms in brackets and provide cross-references under the pseudonyms, or list under pseudonyms and cross-reference from the real name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Creasey, John [Gordon Ashe, pseud.]. A Blast of Trumpets. ——— [Anthony Morton, pseud.]. Hide the Baron. Or alternatively: Ashe, Gordon. See Creasey, John; Creasey, John. See Ashe, Gordon; Morton, Anthony; York, Jeremy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors known by a given name or mononym
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors generally known only by their given names or by a mononym are listed and alphabetized by those names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit titles like “King” or “Saint” and identifiers by place (e.g., “of Hippo”) unless needed for disambiguation. Examples: Augustine. On Christian Doctrine; Elizabeth I. Collected Works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization as author
rubrics_metrics.description: If a publication issued by an organization carries no personal author’s name on the title page, the organization is listed as author in a bibliography, even if it is also given as publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: International Organization for Standardization. Information and Documentation—Rules for the Abbreviation of Title Words and Titles of Publications. (See also exceptions noted elsewhere, e.g., 14.79.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Italics versus quotation marks for titles of cited works
rubrics_metrics.description: Italics are used for the titles of books and journals; quotation marks are generally reserved for titles of subsections of larger works (chapters, articles, poems in a collection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Italics also used for titles of newspapers and blogs, movies and video games, paintings, and other standalone works. Some work types (book series, websites) use neither italics nor quotation marks. For titles within titles, see relevant rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of titles in source citations
rubrics_metrics.description: English-language titles of works are capitalized headline-style in source citations (first and last words and other major words capitalized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See detailed definition at 8.159 for hyphenated compounds and more examples. For non-English titles, sentence-style capitalization is recommended (see separate rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible changes to titles of cited works
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserve the spelling, hyphenation, and punctuation in the original title with specified exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: words in full capitals (except initialisms/acronyms) set in upper- and lower-case; apply headline-style capitalization; ampersand may be changed to and at editorial discretion; numbers should remain as in original unless consistency merits change. Punctuation separating title and subtitle may be adjusted. For older titles see 14.97.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of colon to separate main title and subtitle
rubrics_metrics.description: A colon is used to separate the main title from the subtitle (even if no colon appears in the source itself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A space follows the colon. In italicized titles the colon is also italicized. The subtitle always begins with a capital letter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two subtitles formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are two subtitles in the original, a colon normally precedes the first and a semicolon the second; the second subtitle also begins with a capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Cries Unheard: Why Children Kill; The Story of Mary Bell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Em dash as part of title
rubrics_metrics.description: An em dash is usually considered part of a title or subtitle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain em dashes where they appear in the original title. Example: Crucible of Command: Ulysses S. Grant and Robert E. Lee—the War They Fought, the Peace They Forged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of “or” with double titles
rubrics_metrics.description: For old-fashioned double titles connected by or, prefer the punctuation on the title page; if not available or the original is not consulted use a simpler modern form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize the first word of the subtitle following or. Examples: The Tempest, or The Enchanted Island; Moby-Dick; or, The Whale; Dr. Strangelove, or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling tags like “and other stories”
rubrics_metrics.description: Tags such as and other stories are treated as part of the main title but usually separated from the title story by a comma, even when such a comma does not appear on the title page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first part of the title is not enclosed in quotation marks. If the main title ends with ? or !, omit the comma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dates in titles
rubrics_metrics.description: When not introduced by a preposition, dates in a title or subtitle are set off by commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a colon separates title and subtitle in the original, retain it. Do not add commas to non-English titles before dates. Example: After Hegel: German Philosophy, 1840-1900.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quoted titles within an italicized title
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of long or short works appearing within an italicized title are enclosed in quotation marks, regardless of how those titles would appear alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Think Like a Freak: The Authors of “Freakonomics” Offer to Retrain Your Brain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicized terms within an italicized title (reverse italics)
rubrics_metrics.description: When terms normally italicized in running text (species names, ship names, words in another language) appear within an italicized title, they are set in roman (reverse italics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such a term makes up the entire title, italicize it. Example: The Big E: The Story of the USS Enterprise (USS Enterprise in roman within an italicized title).

rubrics_metrics.name: Question marks and exclamation points in titles
rubrics_metrics.description: When a main title ends with a question mark or an exclamation point, no colon is added before any subtitle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the question/exclamation is followed by a closing quotation mark, retain a colon before the subtitle. Omit a period that would normally follow the title when it ends with ? or !. Retain other punctuation required by surrounding text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Older and very long titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles published in the eighteenth century or earlier may retain their original punctuation, spelling, and capitalization (except whole words in capitals reduced to initial caps). Very long titles may be shortened in a bibliography or a note using bracketed ellipses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bracketed ellipses signal supplied omissions and must be followed by a period at the end of a title abbreviation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of non-English titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentence-style capitalization is strongly recommended for non-English titles (capitalize the first word and any word that would be capitalized in the original language).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain an initial definite article because it may govern inflection. Months and abbreviations like no. or pt. are usually given in English. If unfamiliar with the language, seek expert help or consult a catalog entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translated titles and indicating original language
rubrics_metrics.description: If an English translation of a title is needed, it follows the original title in brackets, without italics or quotation marks, and is capitalized sentence-style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a title is given only in English translation, specify the original language (e.g., [in Russian]). Published translations are treated like any other edition (see examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements to include when citing a book
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference to a book must include enough information to lead readers to the source; typical elements are: author, title, editor/compiler/translator, edition (if not first), volume information, series title/number, publication facts (city, publisher, date), page numbers (if applicable), and URL/DOI for online books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order and presence of elements vary by type of book; these elements are included where applicable in full notes and bibliography entries. See chapter 15 for author-date variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of author's name and title in source citations
rubrics_metrics.description: An author’s name and the title of a book should generally be cited according to how they appear on the title page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a bibliography the first-listed author’s name is normally inverted. Use the form that appears on the title page unless other rules (e.g., initials vs full names) dictate otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-English bibliographic terms and abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: When books in another language are cited in English-language works, bibliographic terms (volume, edition) may be translated but it is often wiser to leave them in the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviations such as Bd. and t. that appear in library catalogs may be left as is. If in doubt, check a major catalog (Library of Congress, WorldCat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor in place of author
rubrics_metrics.description: When no author appears on the title page, list the work by the name(s) of the editor(s), compiler(s), or translator(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In full notes and bibliographies, follow the name with the abbreviation ed. or eds., comp. or comps., or trans., preceded by a comma. In shortened notes and text citations the abbreviation is omitted. Example: Jennifer Egan, ed., The Best American Short Stories, 2014.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor or translator in addition to author
rubrics_metrics.description: If an editor, compiler, or translator is listed on the title page in addition to an author, their name(s) appear after the title preceded by edited by or ed., compiled by or comp., or translated by or trans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plural forms eds. and comps. are never used in this position. Edited by (or similar) is usually spelled out in bibliographies but abbreviated in notes. If both translator and editor are listed, present them in the same order as the title page. Simplify overly long title-page phrases to Edited by or Translated by where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listing by editor when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasionally, when an editor or translator is more important to the discussion than the original author, a book may be listed under the editor’s name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Eliot, T. S., ed. Literary Essays. By Ezra Pound. Use judgment about which name better serves readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other contributors listed on title page
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of people other than author, editor, compiler, or translator may be included in a full note or bibliography if they are significant to a reader’s assessment of the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For ghostwritten books use with. For forewords/intros, include the contributor if considered important. Accurately convey title-page information. Example: With a foreword by Carol Burnett.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chapter in a single-author book citation
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing a specific chapter or part of a single-author book, list the author, chapter title (in quotation marks), followed by in and the book title in italics; give inclusive page numbers or chapter/part number as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either the chapter or the book may be listed first in the bibliography. Example note: Kate Andersen Brower, “Backstairs Gossip and Mischief,” in The Residence: Inside the Private World of the White House, 211.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution to a multiauthor book
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing one contribution to a multiauthor book, begin with the contributor’s name, the title of the contribution in roman (in quotation marks in notes), followed by in and the book title in italics, then the editor(s) and inclusive page numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the bibliography give inclusive page numbers. If multiple contributions to the same multiauthor book are cited, the book itself may be listed with cross-references to individual contributions to avoid clutter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book-length work within a book
rubrics_metrics.description: If the cited part of a book would normally be italicized if published alone (a play, novella), it may be italicized rather than enclosed in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Thomas Bernhard, A Party for Boris, in Histrionics: Three Plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introductions, prefaces, afterwords (generic parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reference is to a generic title such as introduction, preface, or afterword, that term (lowercased unless following a period) is added before the title of the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the author of the introduction is someone other than the main author, list that author first and then the book author after the title. Include page-range for the part in a bibliography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters in published collections
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference to a letter in a published collection begins with the names of the sender and the recipient (in that order), followed by a date and sometimes the place; the title of the collection is given in the usual form for a book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words like letter, postcard, email are usually unnecessary. For unpublished communications see 14.214. When a single letter is included in a bibliography, list it under the writer’s name only.
